Patient Vignette: Mr. T. (Age 63, Financial Analyst)

Mr. T. is a 63-year-old married man of Oceania descent who presents for consultation at the urging of his wife. He is a meticulous, soft-spoken man who has worked as a financial analyst for thirty-seven years, and he arrives for his sessions directly from the office, still wearing a pressed, conservative suit. He sits with his hands folded, his posture rigid, and he often checks his watch. He describes himself as a "planner," a man who has spent a lifetime calculating probabilities and mitigating risk. He says he came to therapy because his wife is "worried about my nerves," but he is unsure if talking will help.

Six months ago, Mr. T. was driving home from a quarterly earnings meeting on a rainy highway. A tractor-trailer drifted into his lane at high speed. He recalls the moment with a chilling, photographic clarity: the hiss of the wet tires, the blinding glare of the headlights, the sound of the truck's air horn, and the certain knowledge, in the split second before impact, that he was going to die. His car spun, rolled twice, and came to rest upside down in a muddy median. He was trapped for forty minutes before being cut free. He sustained a fractured clavicle and three broken ribs, but no head injury. He was discharged from the hospital after two days.

Physically, he has healed. But the world has not.

At work, Mr. T. was once known for his calm, analytical demeanor-the man who could see patterns in chaos. Now, the open-plan office is a landscape of threat. He cannot bear to have his back to a door. He has rearranged his desk, pushing it into a corner so he can see every entrance. When a colleague drops a binder, Mr. T. flinches so violently that he knocks his coffee cup across his spreadsheets. The sound of a truck reversing outside his window sends a jolt of electricity down his spine, and he has to excuse himself to the restroom to breathe. He finds himself unable to focus on the numbers; his mind is constantly scanning, listening for the next threat. His productivity has plummeted. For the first time in his career, he has missed deadlines.

He no longer drives. He takes the train to work, but even that is a trial. He chooses a seat facing forward, near the emergency exit, and he spends the entire ride tensed, gripping the armrest, watching the driver's reflection in the glass. Any sudden braking causes his heart to pound so hard he feels dizzy. His wife does the grocery shopping now, and she drives them everywhere. He feels a deep, gnawing shame about this, about his dependency, but the thought of getting behind the wheel again fills him with an irrational, absolute terror.

The nights are the worst. He is exhausted, but sleep eludes him. He lies awake, listening to the house settle, his body braced for a crash that will not come. When he does sleep, he is pulled into the same dream: the wet road, the headlights, the sound of twisting metal. He wakes in a cold sweat, his hands shaking. He gets up and walks through the dark house, checking the locks on the doors and windows, sometimes three or four times. He knows it is unreasonable, but the compulsion is stronger than his logic.

He has become irritable with his wife, snapping at her for small things-a dish left in the sink, a question about his day. He feels a constant, low-level pressure in his chest, as if he is waiting for the other shoe to drop. He has stopped seeing his grandchildren, because the drive to their house is too long, and the noise and chaos of their play make him feel trapped and panicked.

Mr. T. is a man who built his life on the belief that careful planning could control outcomes. The accident shattered that belief. He now lives in a world where safety is an illusion, where a truck can appear from nowhere, where his own body and mind have become the enemy. He is not sure how to rebuild a life on ground he no longer trusts.
